props.name: countries
props.doc: Countries offered by the dial-code Select. When omitted, uses the built-in curated list.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: Placeholder of the tel input. Falls back to the selected country's mask when empty.

props.name: size
props.doc: Size forwarded to the InputGroup and the dial-code Select trigger. Heights: small=28px, medium=32px, large=40px.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables both the dial-code Select and the internal input.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: Marks the internal input read-only; dial-code Select is also disabled while readonly.

props.name: required
props.doc: Applies the required border on the InputGroup and sets required on the input.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: Applies the invalid border on the InputGroup and sets aria-invalid on the input.

props.name: name
props.doc: HTML name for the internal input (form + vee-validate integration).

props.name: searchPlaceholder
props.doc: Placeholder of the search box that filters the dial-code list. Empty uses the locale catalog (`Search country`).

props.name: searchEmptyLabel
props.doc: Shown in the dial-code list when no country matches the search. Empty uses the locale catalog (`No country found`).

events.name: update:phone
events.notes: One-way snapshot of the number, emitted once on mount and again whenever the digits or the country change. `PhoneNumber` (exported from the component) is `{ country: string; dialCode: string; digits: string; number: string; complete: boolean }`: `number` is the full E.164 number (`dialCode + digits`, e.g. `'+5511999999999'`; `''` while empty) and `complete` is true when the digit count is one the selected country allows. Not a v-model — the field never reads it back.

phone-input.purpose: International phone-number control: an `InputGroup` with a searchable dial-code `Select` on the left and a `type="tel"` input on the right that applies the selected country's mask as the user types and accepts exactly the lengths that country allows. Two v-models (`v-model` for the national digits, `v-model:country` for the ISO 3166-1 alpha-2 code) carry the editable state; the one-way `update:phone` event hands the form the full E.164 number and whether it is complete. It carries no label or helper text: wrap it in a `Field` (it replaces the v5 `field-phone-number`), and it picks up `id`, `aria-describedby`, `invalid`, `disabled` and `required` from the Field.
useWhen: International phone entry where the user picks a country and types the national number with that country's mask.
Forms that need the full E.164 number and whether it is complete, without per-country length rules in the form.
avoidWhen: The value may include characters the masks reject (extensions, free-form notes) → use `input`.
The input needs addons other than the dial code → use `input-group` and compose it yourself.
related: field` — wraps the control with its label, description and error.
input-group` — the container this control renders around the dial-code select and the input.
select` — the dial-code picker inside the group.
bestPractices: Put it in a `Field` with a `Field.Label`; the label targets the tel input.
v-model` holds the national digits only; read `number` from the `update:phone` payload when you need the E.164 value.
Use `complete` from `update:phone` to decide `invalid` and the `Field.Error` on submit; the control shows no incomplete-number message of its own.
v-model:country` defaults to `'BR'`; seed it with the user's country when you know it.
searchPlaceholder` and `searchEmptyLabel` default to English; pass translated copy in localized UIs.

props.name: label
props.doc: Fallback text when the default slot is empty.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Visual variant; `disabled` also prepends a `pi pi-lock` icon.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Helper text; falls back to `label` prop when empty.

helper-text.purpose: Auxiliary text rendered below a form input to communicate guidance (`helper`), validation errors (`invalid`), required-field reminders (`required`), or a locked/disabled state (`disabled`). Each variant changes only color (and, for `disabled`, prepends a lock icon) so the visual weight stays consistent with the field above it.
useWhen: Guidance under a bare input you compose yourself (format hints, limits).
A validation error (`kind="invalid"`), a required reminder (`kind="required"`), or a locked-field notice (`kind="disabled"`) under a field.
avoidWhen: A standard form field → use `field`, whose `Field.Description` / `Field.Error` render this helper and wire it to the control.
The field name or required marker above the input → use `label`.
Feedback about a whole form or page rather than one field → use `message`.
related: label` — sits above the input; HelperText sits below it.
field` — `Field.Description` switches the helper `kind` from the Field's `disabled`, `invalid` and `required` state.
message` — banner-level feedback with severity and an optional action.
bestPractices: Give it an `id` and point the input's `aria-describedby` at it so screen readers read it with the field.
Pick `kind` from the field state: `invalid` for errors, `required` for a missing required value, `disabled` when the field is locked.
Keep it to one short line; `kind="disabled"` already prepends the lock icon, so do not add another.

props.name: text
props.doc: Guidance text revealed on hover or focus; also the trigger's accessible name.

props.name: placement
props.doc: Anchor side of the tooltip relative to the glyph.

hint.purpose: Small info affordance — a muted `pi pi-info-circle` glyph on a focusable button — that reveals one short explanation on hover or focus, through `Tooltip`. It is the standard way to attach a "why does this matter?" note to a field name without spending a line of vertical space on it, and it is what `Label`'s `hint` prop renders.
useWhen: A field, switch or setting whose name is clear but whose consequence is not (what "Sensitive" does to a stored value).
A short, self-contained sentence — one that reads fine in a tooltip and is not needed to complete the field.
Beside a label, a section heading, or a table column header, where a permanent line of helper text would add noise.
avoidWhen: Guidance the user needs while typing, or any validation message → use `helper-text` (it stays on screen and is wired with `aria-describedby`).
More than a sentence, links, or formatted content → use `popover`, which is dismissible and can hold real content.
A plain description of an action already labelled by a control → use `tooltip` directly on that control.
related: tooltip` — the overlay `Hint` composes; reach for it when the trigger is an existing control rather than a standalone info glyph.
helper-text` — persistent guidance under a field; the right choice when the text must always be visible.
label` — renders `Hint` from its own `hint` prop, so a field name and its note stay one component.
bestPractices: One sentence, ending in a period. If it needs two, it belongs in `helper-text` or a `popover`.
Never hide required information behind a hint — hover is not discoverable on touch, so treat it as an enhancement.
The `text` doubles as the button's accessible name, so write it as prose a screen reader can read verbatim.
Place it immediately after the thing it explains, not at the end of a row.

props.name: label
props.doc: Fallback text when the default slot is empty.

props.name: required
props.doc: Appends an inline required indicator (`* (Required)`) next to the label text. The `*` uses `var(--primary)`; "(Required)" inherits `var(--text-muted)`.

props.name: hint
props.doc: Short explanation appended as a `Hint` glyph that reveals it on hover or focus. Empty renders no glyph.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Label text; falls back to `label` prop when empty.

label.purpose: Form-field label that pairs descriptive text with an optional required indicator and an optional hint. Renders a native `<label>` element so consumers can associate it with any input via the standard `for` attribute. Use it above (or beside) any input control in the `inputs` category to communicate the field name and whether it must be filled. The required indicator is rendered inline as `* (Required)` — the `*` in the primary orange followed by the parenthesized word "(Required)" in muted text — replacing the older `Tag` badge for a lighter typographic signal. Setting `hint` appends a `Hint` glyph after the text, so a field name and its one-sentence explanation stay one component instead of a hand-built row.
useWhen: Naming a bare input when you compose a field layout yourself.
Marking a field as required with the inline `* (Required)` indicator.
Attaching a one-sentence explanation to a field name with `hint`.
avoidWhen: A standard text, password, select, or textarea field → use `field`, whose `Field.Label` targets the control and shows the Required marker for you.
Guidance, error, or required messages under the input → use `helper-text`.
An info glyph with no field name next to it → use `hint`.
related: helper-text` — the line under the input; pairs with the label above it.
hint` — the glyph the `hint` prop renders; use it alone when there is no label.
field` — composes label, any control, and description/error with the wiring done.
bestPractices: Always set `for` to the input's id (`inputId` on the bare inputs) so clicking the label focuses the control.
required` is visual only; also set `required` on the input so it carries `aria-required`.
Keep `hint` to one short sentence; it is revealed in a tooltip on hover or focus.
Pass the text through `label` or the default slot, not both; the slot wins.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Two-way bound value of the field.

props.name: placeholder
props.doc: Placeholder shown when the field is empty.

props.name: maxLength
props.doc: Native `maxlength` — maximum number of characters allowed.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies disabled tokens. The toggle button inherits the disabled state.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: Marks the field read-only; value is visible but not editable. Toggle button stays operable.

props.name: required
props.doc: Marks the field as required; sets native `required` and `aria-required`. Visual indicator (asterisk) is owned by the wrapping form-field, not by this component.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: Applies the invalid border + ring tokens and sets `aria-invalid`.

props.name: toggleable
props.doc: When true, renders the visibility toggle button on the trailing edge of the field. When false, the field behaves as a plain password input with no toggle and the `iconRight` slot becomes available.

props.name: autocomplete
props.doc: Native `autocomplete` hint for password managers. Use `new-password` for sign-up and password-change flows.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: Emitted on native `input` event with the new value.

slots.name: iconLeft
slots.notes: Leading icon rendered inside the field, before the input. Hidden from assistive tech (`aria-hidden="true"`).

slots.name: iconRight
slots.notes: Trailing icon rendered inside the field, after the input. **Only honored when `toggleable=false`** — the visibility toggle occupies this slot when enabled. Hidden from assistive tech (`aria-hidden="true"`).

password-input.purpose: Single-line password input for forms. Renders a bordered field with a built-in visibility toggle button on the trailing edge that flips the native `type` between `password` and `text`. Shares the visual language of `Input` (same heights, borders, focus ring, disabled treatment). The component is the field only — labels, helper text, and strength meters live in the wrapping form-field layer. Aligned with Figma frame `3714:10788` (Webkit / PasswordInput). The token mapping was originally inferred from the `input` sibling because the Figma MCP was unreachable during spec authoring; it has since been **reconciled against the frame** as rendered inside the password field frame (`2027:3212`), which corrected the trailing padding to `var(--spacing-xs)` and the visibility toggle to the 28 px (`small`) `IconButton`. One frame value is deliberately not adopted: the border width stays at the shared 1 px rather than the frame's `var(--border-width-default)` (0.8 px), because this component's contract is to share `Input`'s borders and `Input` is still on 1 px — moving one without the other would break that stated invariant. Adopting it is a coordinated follow-up across every bordered input.
useWhen: A bare password field whose label and errors are laid out separately (an inline re-authentication prompt, a custom form row).
Any secret the user may need to check while typing (passwords, tokens); the built-in toggle reveals it as plain text.
avoidWhen: A password field with a label, helper or error text, or a requirements row → wrap it in a `field` (with `password-requirements` for the rules row).
The value is not secret → use `input`.
related: field` — wraps this input with its label and description; it hands the input its id, `aria-describedby` and state.
password-requirements` — the live checklist of password rules rendered under this input.
input` — plain-text field with the same borders, focus ring, and disabled treatment.
input` — plain single-line text input.
bestPractices: Set `autocomplete="new-password"` on sign-up and password-change forms; keep the default `current-password` on login.
Leave `toggleable` on; turn it off only when you need the `iconRight` slot, which is ignored while the toggle is shown.
The field is a fixed 40px tall with no `size` prop; align it with `size="large"` siblings in the same row.
Give it an accessible name: a `label` whose `for` matches an `id` passed to the input, or `aria-label`.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Placement. Inline is an always-visible dashed region; overlay stays hidden until files are dragged over the window, then covers its nearest positioned ancestor.

props.name: title
props.doc: Instruction shown under the icon. Empty uses the locale catalog (`Drop files to upload`).

props.name: description
props.doc: Secondary line under the title, typically the accepted types and limits. Not rendered when empty.

props.name: accept
props.doc: Comma-separated file filter using the native input accept syntax (extensions, MIME types, type wildcards). Files that do not match are rejected. Empty accepts every file.

props.name: multiple
props.doc: When false, only the first accepted file of a drop is accepted and the rest are rejected.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Ignores drags and drops: no active state, no events.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: Paints the inline region with the danger border so a wrapping field can show a validation error. Drops still work.

props.name: icon
props.doc: PrimeIcons class for the glyph above the title.

events.name: drop
events.notes: Activation event. Fires when files are dropped on the target (the inline root, or the visible overlay) and at least one passes `accept` / `multiple`. `files` holds only the accepted files, in `dataTransfer.files` order, and is never empty. Not emitted when `disabled`. Declaring `drop` means a consumer `@drop` listener binds to this event, never to the native DOM `drop` on the root.

events.name: reject
events.notes: Activation event. Fires on the same drop when one or more files were filtered out, because they do not match `accept` or exceed `multiple="false"`. `files` holds only the rejected files and is never empty. When a drop has both kinds of file, `drop` fires first, then `reject`, with the same `event`. Not emitted when `disabled`.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Actions or extra content under the description, typically a "Browse files" `Button`. Rendered only in `kind="inline"`. The overlay is `aria-hidden` decoration, so interactive content there would be unreachable and is not rendered.

file-dropzone.purpose: A FileDropzone is the target a user drags files from the operating system onto. It owns the drag lifecycle (only drags carrying `Files` count), the `accept` / `multiple` filtering, and the idle/active look, and it hands the result back as two activation events: `drop` with the accepted files, `reject` with the files it filtered out. It holds no value and renders no file list. The list, upload progress and validation messages belong to the consumer (typically a `Field` around this component, whose `Field.Description` / `Field.Error` carry the messages). `kind` covers the two places a drop target lives: - **`inline`**: a dashed region that is always visible (icon, title, description, plus a default slot for the "Browse files" action the consumer composes). It switches to the active look while files are dragged over it. This is the Cloudscape FileDropzone / Cloudflare Pages "Upload assets" shape. - **`overlay`**: invisible at rest. When files are dragged into the window it fades in over its nearest positioned ancestor (`absolute inset-0`), and it fades out on window drag-leave, drop or `Escape`. This is the Vercel "drag and drop a folder to deploy" shape, and it replaces the sample app's page-level `ProjectDropZone` and the drop target in the `Templates/Platform/States/ProjectIntake` story. The drop target itself is pointer-only. It is never a keyboard control. The keyboard (and screen-reader) path to the same outcome is a real button the consumer puts in the default slot (`inline`), or elsewhere on the page (`overlay`).
useWhen: A form or settings surface accepts one or more files and should also accept them by drag (`kind="inline"` with a Browse button in the slot).
A whole page or card should accept a project, folder contents or assets dropped anywhere on it, with no permanent drop region taking up space (`kind="overlay"` inside a `relative` container).
The consumer needs the accepted and rejected files separated by an `accept` filter before it uploads anything.
avoidWhen: Picking files by keyboard or click only, with no drag affordance → a `button` that opens a native file input is enough.
Showing the chosen files, their progress or their errors → render them yourself with `progress`, `message` or `helper-text`. The dropzone renders none of these.
Dragging items inside the page (reordering rows, moving cards) → this component only reacts to OS drags that carry `Files`. In-page drag and drop is out of scope.
A static "nothing here yet" panel with no drop behavior → use `empty-state`.
related: button`: the "Browse files" action composed into the default slot. It is the keyboard path to the same outcome as a drop.
empty-state`: a no-data panel. Compose a FileDropzone inside or beside it when the empty state's call to action is "upload".
progress`: the consumer renders per-file progress after `drop`. The dropzone does not track uploads.
toast`: confirms the result of a drop or reports rejected files to everyone, including users who never see the drag.
card`: a positioned container (`class="relative"`) that hosts an `overlay` dropzone.
bestPractices: Always give the user a non-drag path. In `inline`, put a `Button` in the default slot that opens a native `<input type="file">`. In `overlay`, keep an upload button somewhere on the page. The drop target is pointer-only by design.
Pass the same `accept` string to the dropzone and to the native input behind your Browse button, so both paths filter the same way.
Handle `reject`. Tell the user which files were skipped and why (e.g. a `toast` naming the files and the accepted types). A silent rejection reads as a broken drop.
Announce the outcome of a drop yourself (a toast, or a live region on your file list). The dropzone does not announce drag states (see Accessibility).

Render one `overlay` dropzone per positioned container, and make the container `relative`. Without a positioned ancestor the overlay covers the nearest positioned element up the tree, which may be the whole page.
Place the `overlay` dropzone as the last child of its container, so it paints above the container's other positioned content (see Theme gaps).
When the consumer's own flow is busy (an upload in progress), set `disabled` and disable the Browse button too.
Put the accepted types and limits in `description` ("PNG or JPG, up to 5 MB"). The title is the instruction, the description is the constraint.

password-requirements.treeShakeableNote: No tree-shakeable root. Add "./password-requirements-root" -> the root .vue, or import sub-components individually.

props.name: requirements
props.doc: Rules rendered as chips, one per entry. Defaults to the built-in rule set; an empty array renders only the caption.

props.name: title
props.doc: Caption that opens the row and names the group for assistive tech. Empty uses the locale catalog (`Must contain:`).

props.name: value
props.doc: Password every rule is evaluated against; pass the PasswordInput value.

password-requirements.purpose: Live checklist of password rules shown under a `PasswordInput`: a caption followed by one chip per rule, each chip turning to the success tone with a check as the typed value satisfies it. It replaces the requirements row of the v5 `field-password`; the entry also exports `DEFAULT_PASSWORD_REQUIREMENTS` and the `PasswordRequirement` type so a form validates with the same rules it shows.
useWhen: A new-password field (sign-up, reset, change password) where the user must meet explicit rules.
avoidWhen: A sign-in password field → render `password-input` alone; the rules do not apply to an existing password.
A free-form strength meter → not provided; compose your own.
related: password-input` — the control whose value this checklist evaluates.
field` — place both inside one `Field` so the label and description stay together.
bestPractices: Bind `value` to the same ref as the `PasswordInput` `v-model`.
Validate on submit with `DEFAULT_PASSWORD_REQUIREMENTS` (or your own array) so the error and the chips never disagree.
Pass `requirements` to replace the rule set and `title` to localize the caption.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Currently selected item value (v-model).

props.name: items
props.doc: Options rendered as selectable cards; each entry must include `value` and `label`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables all options and applies disabled tokens.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: v-model when the user selects an option.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Overrides the entire card body for an option.

slots.name: tag
slots.notes: Trailing content below label/description (e.g. plan badge).

radio-cards.purpose: Horizontal grid of selectable cards for mutually exclusive choices (plans, roles, feature tiers). Each option shows label, optional icon and description, with optional trailing content via the `tag` slot. Migrated from the legacy `radio-cards` core component into the webkit inputs layer.
useWhen: One choice among a few options where each option needs a label plus an optional icon or one-line description: usage intent, role, plan tier.
Options laid out side by side as cards that wrap onto new rows, bound to one `v-model` value for the whole group.
A card needs small trailing content under its text, such as a price or a "Recommended" tag, through the `tag` slot.
avoidWhen: You place each card-style radio by hand, or the choice must submit through a native form `name` → use `field` choice cards (`Field.Label` wrapping a horizontal `Field` with a `radio-button`).
The options don't need card weight and read fine as inline rows → use horizontal `field`s with a `radio-button`.
There are more options than fit in a row or two, or the choice sits in a compact form → use `select` inside a `field`.
More than one option can be picked → use `field` choice cards with a `checkbox`.
related: field` — a `Field.Label` choice card is a single card-style radio (or checkbox) with title and description; compose several by hand with a shared `name`, or use a horizontal `Field` for an inline labelled row.
select` — dropdown for long option lists.
onboarding-form` — uses this component for its usage-intent question.
bestPractices: Give every item a unique `value`; it is both the `v-model` payload and the render key.

Name the group by passing `aria-labelledby` or `aria-label` on the component: it renders a `role="radiogroup"` with no visible label of its own. Set an item's `ariaLabel` when its `label` alone is ambiguous.
disabled` applies to the whole group; there is no per-item disabled state, so leave unavailable options out of `items`.
Use the `tag` slot for trailing content. The `default` slot replaces the whole card body (icon, label, description and `tag`), so use it only when the card needs a different layout.
Arrow keys move and select in one step, as in any radio group, so `update:modelValue` fires while a keyboard user browses. Don't trigger navigation or requests on every change.

props.name: label
props.doc: Fallback text when the default slot is empty.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Visual variant. Filled is an applied value, outlined an available one, dashed the control that adds one.

props.name: size
props.doc: Size token; `small` is a fixed 24px, `medium` a fixed 32px.

props.name: removable
props.doc: When true, renders a trailing remove button that emits `remove`.

props.name: clickable
props.doc: When true, the chip body becomes interactive (`role="button"`, focusable) and emits `click` on activation (click / Enter / Space).

props.name: selectable
props.doc: When true, the chip becomes a toggle: activating it flips the `selected` model and emits `click`.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Suppresses activation, toggling and removal.

events.name: remove
events.notes: Fires when `removable` is true and the remove button is activated (click / Enter / Space), **immediately** — the chip does not hide or unmount itself first, so the consumer decides whether the chip disappears, stays, or becomes an `outlined` offer. `label` is the chip's `label` prop, identifying which chip was removed.

events.name: click
events.notes: Fires only when `clickable` or `selectable` is true, `disabled` is false, and the chip body is activated — by pointer, or `Enter` / `Space` while the root is focused. `label` identifies which chip was clicked. When `selectable`, the `selected` model is already flipped when `click` fires. The trailing remove button stops propagation, so activating it emits `remove` only, never `click`. `update:selected` comes from `v-model:selected` (see above).

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Chip content; falls back to `label` when empty.

chip.purpose: A Chip is a compact, pill-shaped token that labels a discrete value the user has applied — most often a filter on a data view. Unlike `tag` (a read-only status/category badge with severity color coding), a Chip carries no severity and exposes an optional trailing remove control: when `removable` is set, it renders a real `<button>` that emits `remove`, so the consumer can drop the value from a collection. This is the token consumed by the data table's `#filters` slot (`<Chip :label="f.label" removable @remove="dropFilter(f)" />`): each active filter becomes one removable Chip, and dismissing it removes that filter. Reach for a Chip when a value is user-applied and dismissible; reach for `tag` when it is a static status or category indicator. `kind` covers the three jobs a chip does in a filter surface, so a consumer never restyles the component to get one of them: - **`filled`** — a value that IS applied. The shared surface and border plus `--shadow-sm`: the loudest of the three, because it is state. - **`outlined`** — a value the user COULD apply. Same surface and border, no shadow: it recedes to an offer without becoming disabled, so a filter vocabulary can stay on screen instead of hiding inside a menu. - **`dashed`** — the control that CREATES a chip ("Add filter"). A dashed outline is the standing convention for "add another one of these", which is what separates the thing that makes filters from the things that are filters. **Selected is a mode, not a kind.** `selectable` turns the chip into a toggle: activating it flips the `selected` model (`v-model:selected`), and the state stays after the click until the chip is activated again. It is independent of `kind` — `filled` marks an applied filter and never means "selected", so a selectable chip of any kind paints its selected state the same way (`--bg-selected` fill, `--border-selected` outline) and announces it as `aria-pressed`. Reach for `selectable` when a set of chips is a row of toggles (quick filters, facets); keep `clickable` when activation opens or does something without holding a state. **Presence is the consumer's, not the chip's.** `remove` fires the moment the control is activated; the chip does not animate itself away or unmount itself. A chip that hid itself on remove could only ever serve the one case where removing it also destroys it — a filter bar where a removed value stays on screen as an `outlined` offer was impossible, because the instance stayed invisible forever. Exit motion, if wanted, belongs to whatever owns the list (a `TransitionGroup` around the group).
useWhen: Represent a selectable or removable token — active filters, multi-select values, entered keywords.
Represent a value that is _available_ but not applied (`kind="outlined"`), so the set of things a view can be narrowed by stays visible.
Represent the "add another" affordance for such a set (`kind="dashed"`).
Represent a row of toggles that each hold an on/off state (`selectable` + `v-model:selected`).
The element is interactive (clickable / dismissible).
avoidWhen: It is a static count or one-glance status → use `badge`.
It is a static descriptive label/category with no interaction → use `tag`.
related: badge` — static count/short-value indicator.
tag` — static labelled status/category chip.
tooltip` — composed by the remove control to name what it removes.
bestPractices: When removable, expose an accessible remove control with a clear label.
Group related chips in a `chip-group` rather than ad-hoc layout.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Two-way bound value. Boolean in `binary` mode, scalar when paired with `value`, array when multi-selecting.

props.name: value
props.doc: Identifier for this checkbox in non-binary mode. Compared against `modelValue` (or included in the array).

props.name: binary
props.doc: When true, the checkbox toggles `modelValue` as a boolean (no `value` pairing).

props.name: indeterminate
props.doc: Renders the indeterminate visual (horizontal bar). Does not affect `modelValue`; the parent owns the tri-state logic.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies disabled tokens.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: Marks the field read-only; value is visible but cannot change via interaction.

props.name: inputId
props.doc: Forwarded to the inner `<input id>` for label association.

props.name: name
props.doc: HTML name for form submission.

props.name: tabindex
props.doc: Forwarded to the inner `<input tabindex>`.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: Fires on activation. Payload is the next boolean (binary mode) or the next array (every other mode).

checkbox.purpose: Binary selection control. Supports a single boolean (`binary: true`) and array-based multi-select (adds or removes its `value` in the `modelValue` array) (used by `MultiSelect` and `DataTable` to drive bulk selection). The new `indeterminate` prop renders a third visual state (horizontal bar) and sets `aria-checked="mixed"` — used by parents that own a partial-selection summary (e.g. "select all" rows where some children are selected). Aligned with Figma frame `2027:7311`.
useWhen: A bare boolean control whose label lives outside it: a table row-selection cell, an option row in a list, a settings matrix.
Picking several values from a short set: give each box its own `value` and bind them all to one array `v-model`.
A "select all" control over a partial selection: set `indeterminate` while only some children are checked.
avoidWhen: A form field that needs its own label, description, or helper text → wrap it in a horizontal `field` (`Field orientation="horizontal"` + `Field.Content`).
Each option needs a bordered card with a label and description → use a `field` choice card (`Field.Label` wrapping a horizontal `Field`).
An on/off setting that applies as soon as it flips → use `switch`.
Only one option of the set may be chosen → use `radio-button`.
related: field` — `orientation="horizontal"` puts the checkbox beside its label and description (the default inside forms); a `Field.Label` wrapping that Field turns it into a bordered choice card.
switch` — on/off toggle for settings that take effect immediately.
multi-select` — renders this checkbox in every option row; use it when the option list is long.
table` — uses this checkbox for row selection and the select-all header.
bestPractices: Set `binary` for a plain true/false value; without it the checkbox adds or removes its `value` in an array `modelValue`.
Give every checkbox an accessible name: point a `label` element's `for` at `inputId`, or pass `aria-label` (attributes land on the inner input).
indeterminate` only changes the visual and sets `aria-checked="mixed"`; the parent computes it and decides what a click does.
Use `readonly` for a value that cannot change in this context and `disabled` for an option that is unavailable.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Selected value for v-model.

props.name: value
props.doc: Option value for this radio instance.

props.name: name
props.doc: HTML name shared across a mutually exclusive group.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies disabled tokens.

props.name: inputId
props.doc: id for the native input; links label to control.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: v-model.

radio-button.purpose: Atomic exclusive-choice control only — the circular radio input from Figma (no label, description, or helper). Wrap it in a horizontal `Field`, or a `Field.Label` choice card, for labeled layouts.
useWhen: One choice from a small set of mutually exclusive options whose labels are laid out separately (a table row, a custom option row).
A custom radio layout that the horizontal `Field` and the `Field.Label` choice card do not cover.
avoidWhen: A radio option in a form that needs its own label, description, or helper text → wrap it in a horizontal `field` (`Field orientation="horizontal"` + `Field.Content`).
Options that need visual weight, such as plans or tiers → use a `field` choice card (`Field.Label` wrapping a horizontal `Field`), or `radio-cards` for a horizontal grid of cards.
More than one option may be selected → use `checkbox`.
The options are many or loaded from data → use `select`.
related: field` — a horizontal `Field` puts the radio beside its label and description (the default inside forms); a `Field.Label` wrapping it is a card-style option with a selected border and background. Group the options in `Field.Set` + `Field.Legend`.
radio-cards` — horizontal grid of selectable cards with its own model.
checkbox` — the multi-pick counterpart.
select` — single choice from a dropdown when the options do not fit inline.
bestPractices: Bind every radio in a group to the same `v-model` and give them the same `name`; each one emits its own `value` when selected.
value` and `modelValue` are strings; map numeric or object ids to strings before binding.
Give each radio an accessible name: point a `label` element's `for` at `inputId`, or pass `aria-label`.
Wrap the group in a `fieldset` with a `legend` so the question itself is announced.

props.name: modelValue
props.doc: Toggled-on state. Bind with `v-model="value"`. Mirrors the Figma checked/on variant.

props.name: kind
props.doc: Visual variant. `privacy` renders a lock icon inside the handle (closed when off, open when on).

props.name: focused
props.doc: Forces the focused visual state regardless of keyboard focus. Mirrors the Figma `focused` variant.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction and applies the disabled tokens.

events.name: update:modelValue
events.notes: Emitted when the user toggles the switch. Paired with `v-model`.

switch.purpose: Control-only pill toggle `Switch` (36×20 px). Two visual types: `default` (plain handle) and `privacy` (handle carries a `pi-lock` / `pi-lock-open` icon mirroring the toggled state). No label or description — wrap it in a horizontal `Field` or a `Field.Label` choice card for labeled layouts, or place it bare where the label already exists outside the control (an ItemGroup row names the field with `Item.Title`). Because the bare form has no wrapper to defer to, the control owns its own `disabled` state.
useWhen: An on/off setting that takes effect as soon as it flips (enable a feature, turn a rule on).
A row that already names the setting outside the control, such as an `item` row whose title is the label.
A visibility or access toggle: `kind="privacy"` shows a closed lock when off and an open lock when on.
avoidWhen: The toggle needs its own label, description, or helper text in a form → wrap it in a horizontal `field` (`Field orientation="horizontal"` + `Field.Content`).
The toggle should sit in a bordered card with a description → use a `field` choice card (`Field.Label` wrapping a horizontal `Field`).
A text value that only applies while a feature is on → compose a `Field` with an `InputGroup` (`InputGroup.Input` + an `InputGroup.Addon` holding the switch).
The choice is submitted with a form instead of applied immediately → use `checkbox`.
related: field` — a horizontal `Field` gives the switch its label and description; a `Field.Label` wrapping it is a card-style option.
input-group` — a text input with a trailing switch addon that enables it, inside a `Field`.
checkbox` — boolean selection submitted with a form.
item` — list row whose title names a bare switch.
bestPractices: The switch renders no text: give it an accessible name with `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby` pointing at the visible label.
Set `disabled` on the switch itself; it renders a native disabled button, so it leaves the tab order and ignores clicks and keys.
focused` moves real focus and forces the ring; use it only to mirror an external focus state, never as decoration.
Keep `kind="default"` unless the setting is about visibility or access.

props.name: min
props.doc: Lowest selectable value; the left end of the track.

props.name: max
props.doc: Highest selectable value; the right end of the track.

props.name: step
props.doc: Increment between selectable values, used by dragging and the arrow keys.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables interaction, removes the control from the tab order and applies the disabled tokens.

props.name: readonly
props.doc: Keeps the control focusable but prevents the value from changing.

props.name: invalid
props.doc: Applies the danger tokens and sets aria-invalid.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name when no visible label is associated with the slider.

props.name: ticks
props.doc: Shows a tick mark at every step when the range has at most 21 positions.

props.name: referenceValues
props.doc: Values marked and labelled under the track; entries outside min and max are ignored.

props.name: unit
props.doc: Text appended verbatim to the reference labels and to the announced value.

events.name: change
events.notes: Commit signal: emitted from the native `change` event — on pointer release after a drag, and after each keyboard step — with the committed value. Lets the consumer persist once per interaction instead of once per drag frame (`update:modelValue` fires continuously). A value event, so no DOM event in the payload (see `.claude/rules/event-payloads.md`). Not emitted while `disabled` or `readonly`.

slider.purpose: Bare range control `Slider`: one thumb on a horizontal track that picks a single number between `min` and `max` in `step` increments, with the portion from `min` to the value filled. It is built on a native `<input type="range">`, so the keyboard model, the `slider` role and the value announcements come from the platform; the component only styles the track, fill and thumb with tokens and adds optional tick marks and labelled reference values under the track. It renders no label, value readout or helper text — a field composes it with `Label` and `HelperText`, the same way `switch` and `number-input` are composed.
useWhen: Picking an approximate value inside a known, bounded range where the position matters more than the exact digit (a spend or usage limit, a percentage threshold, a sampling rate).
A plan or capacity selector whose stops are evenly spaced and few enough to read as tick marks.
A bounded value the user adjusts by feel and then commits (listen to `change` to persist on release instead of on every drag frame).
avoidWhen: The user must type an exact number, or the range is unbounded → use `number-input`.
The choice is between a handful of named options (1h / 24h / 7d) → use `toggle-group`.
An on/off setting → use `switch`.
Showing progress or a read-only quantity the user cannot change → use `progress`.
Selecting a range with two thumbs (from–to) — not supported by this component.
related: number-input` — exact numeric entry; pair it next to a slider when the user needs both coarse dragging and an exact value.
label` — names the slider; point its `for` at the slider's `id` (the `id` attribute lands on the native input).
helper-text` — description or error message under the slider in a field layout.
toggle-group` — a few discrete, named choices instead of a continuous range.
progress` — displays a fraction; it is not interactive.
bestPractices: Always give the slider an accessible name: `aria-label`, or a `Label` whose `for` matches the slider's `id`.
Keep the value inside `[min, max]` and on a `step` multiple; the component clamps the displayed fill but never rewrites the bound value on its own.
Turn on `ticks` only when every step is meaningful and the range has at most 21 positions; above that the ticks are not rendered.
Use `referenceValues` for a few landmarks (`[0, 50, 100]`), not for every step — labels need horizontal room.

Set `unit` when the number alone is ambiguous; it is appended verbatim to the reference labels and to the announced value, so include a leading space for word units (`' GB'`) and none for symbols (`'%'`).
Listen to `change` for expensive side effects (saving a limit to the API); `v-model` updates on every movement.
Use `readonly` to show a value the current user may not change but should still be able to focus and hear; use `disabled` when the control does not apply at all.

props.name: disabled
props.doc: Disables the whole control and applies disabled tokens.

props.name: ariaLabel

dropdown-menu.purpose: Overlay menu that opens from a consumer-supplied trigger and renders a list of selectable options grouped into named sections. The root `DropdownMenu` owns open/closed state, positioning, focus return, and keyboard navigation; `DropdownMenu.Trigger` wires `aria-haspopup`/`aria-expanded`/`aria-controls` onto whatever element the consumer passes through its slot; `DropdownMenu.Group` groups options under an optional label; `DropdownMenu.Option` is the selectable row with left/right/command affordances. useWhen: A menu of actions opened from a button: row actions, an account menu, an overflow ("more") menu.
Options grouped under section labels, optionally with keyboard-shortcut hints.
avoidWhen: Choosing a value that a form submits → use `select` (inside a `field` for a label).
A primary action joined to a menu of alternatives → use `split-button`.
A searchable palette of commands → use `command`.
Free-form or interactive content such as forms or filters → use `popover`.
Vertical application navigation → use `menu`.
related: split-button` — composes `DropdownMenu` for its chevron menu.
select` — form control with a field trigger and a bound value.
popover` — same trigger and anchoring model, with free-form content instead of option rows.
command` — modal ⌘K palette with search and filtering.
bestPractices: Give every `DropdownMenu.Option` a unique `value` and handle the root `select` event as `(event, value)`. The panel closes and focus returns to the trigger on its own.
selected` is a display flag. The dropdown never sets it, so derive it from your own state.
Use the `command` prop or the `right` slot on an option, not both. A `command` shortcut is live only while the panel is open.
Add a `label` to each `DropdownMenu.Group` when there is more than one group. Put search in the root `top` slot and footer actions in `bottom`; those regions stay outside the scrolling list.

multi-select.purpose: Select control specialised for choosing many options from a list. The trigger field mirrors `Input`'s visual API (size, hover/focus/filled/disabled/invalid/required states) so a MultiSelect sits next to other form fields without visual drift. The dropdown panel is teleported to `body` and anchored to the trigger by the shared `usePlacement` composable — no `@floating-ui` runtime. Every option row carries a checkbox indicator (the `Checkbox` webkit component), optionally a leading slot/icon and a trailing tag. Search and "Create new" footer are exposed as slots on `<MultiSelectContent>`. Unlike `Select` (which toggles between single and multi via a `multiple` prop), MultiSelect is multi-only: `modelValue` is always an array and the indicator is always a checkbox. Aligned with Figma frame `3899:29362` (options panel). The trigger reuses the `Input`/`Select` trigger visuals.
useWhen: Choosing several values from a long list (regions, tags, permissions) in a compact field.
A filter whose selected values stay editable from the same dropdown.
Grouped options with icons or trailing tags, optionally with search.
avoidWhen: Only one value may be chosen → use `select`.
A labelled form field with helper/error text → put it (or `select` with `multiple`) inside a `field`.
A handful of options that fit on screen → use a horizontal `field` with a `checkbox` for each.
The user builds a subset and needs the chosen and remaining items side by side → use `pick-list`.
related: select` — single-choice counterpart; also accepts `multiple`.
field` — wraps this control with its label, description and error; it hands the trigger its id and state.
pick-list` — dual-list transfer for building larger subsets.
checkbox` — the indicator every option row renders.
bestPractices: modelValue` is always an array; start it as `[]`, never `null`.
Pass `displayValue` to summarise long selections (e.g. "3 regions") instead of a list that overflows the trigger.
Keep each option's `value` stable and unique; selection is matched by value.
Put a search input in the `search` slot and a create action in the `footer` slot of `MultiSelect.Content`.

footer.purpose: Page footer for marketing and product surfaces: the bottom-of-page counterpart to `GlobalHeader`. A canvas-colored shell divided into bands by hairline rules. Matches the Webkit Footer component set (Figma node 5467:1638, `Type=Default` / `Type=Mobile`). **Four bands.** Top to bottom: the link columns, a row carrying the social icons and the status/language pair, and the signature band (the brand beside its tagline, in its own `FrameBox` with corner marks). **Two placements, chosen with `kind` — the same two `GlobalHeader` has, and the bands are identical in both.** `content` is the default: the bands run full bleed across whatever zone holds the footer, and the footer adds no inset of its own because every band already carries `--spacing-lg` inside it — the value `--layout-boundary-inline` resolves to — so the first column title opens on the page boundary by construction. `site` closes a framed marketing page: the bands take the site column (`layout-column-site`: capped at `--layout-measure-site`, inset by `--layout-boundary-inline` once the window is narrower than that), side rules run down both edges, two hatched `FrameBox` gutters flank them from `2xl`, and a hatched band closes the frame below. Those three hold no content and stay out of the a11y tree. The hero band, the framed sections and this footer resolve to that one measure, which is the only reason the border-x running down the page is continuous; the top bar is deliberately one rung wider (`--layout-measure-site-header`). The frame apparatus belongs to `site` alone, and not as a matter of taste: on a full-bleed footer the side rules land on the zone's own edges, where a hairline reads as a seam against the bezel rather than as a frame, and the `flex-1` gutters — with no slack to grow into — collapse to zero width while still painting their borders and corner marks onto the bands' own edges. **The two Figma variants are one component switching by CSS**, and the switch is not one breakpoint: - The **column grid** folds from four columns to the 2×2 mobile grid below `md` (768px). - The **bands recombine at `md`**: stacked, their order is links → status/language → signature → social icons (the Mobile variant's order); from `md` the social icons and the status pair share one row above the signature. All four bands are cells of **one** grid, so each is a single element in a single place in the DOM at every width — the order is `order-*` when stacked and explicit row/column placement from `md`. A wrapper row that existed only on desktop would mean two copies of the markup, so two copies of the consumer's slot content. - **Row two sizes its two bands by content** (`md:grid-cols-[auto_auto]`), not in half: each band takes what it holds and the two share the slack, so the status pair never wraps while the social band still has room, and the social band wraps only when the zone is narrower than both together. A 50/50 split gave the social band 427px of an 853px docs reading column, 13px short of the brand mark and seven large icons — a premature wrap in every zone narrower than the viewport. - The **gutters appear at `2xl`** (1536px) in the `site` placement, not with the rest of the desktop presentation, because that is the first breakpoint past the measure itself (1388px). props.name: borders
props.doc: Which of the frame's own rules to draw. Takes a keyword, one side, or a list of sides.

props.name: marks
props.doc: Which corner registration squares to draw. Takes a keyword (`all`, `none`, `top`, `bottom`, `left`, `right`), one corner, or a list of corners.

props.name: hatch
props.doc: Show the frame's own linear hatch texture behind the content, faded toward the edges. Prefer `texture-material`'s `lines` kind for a ruled ground; `section-gap` composes that instead.

props.name: flush
props.doc: Which sides a neighbouring frame already draws, so this one does not draw them again. `true` is shorthand for `top`; use `left` for a horizontal row, or a list for a grid cell.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: Frame content; rendered above the hatch texture and stretched to the frame height.

frame-box.purpose: The registration frame: a hairline box with a small square set inside each corner and an optional linear hatch texture behind its content. Every side and every corner is addressable on its own, so frames stack and abut without doubling a rule or a mark. It is the container every framed page section is built from — a section title, the gap between two sections, a cell of a divider grid — so a page's rules and corner marks come from one component instead of from per-screen borders.
useWhen: Wrapping a page section, band, or grid cell that should read as a framed module.
Building a page whose vertical rhythm is drawn by rules rather than by margins: stack frames and let `flush` collapse each junction to a single hairline.
Adding the corner registration marks (and optionally the hatch texture) to an area that already has its rules drawn by a surrounding grid — set `borders="none"` and keep `marks`.
avoidWhen: For a card-shaped surface with padding, a header and a footer → use `card` instead.
For a single separating line between two blocks → use `divider` instead.
For the empty framed band that separates two sections → use `section-gap`, which is this frame configured for that one job.
related: section-gap` — an empty `frame-box` that holds the air between two sections.
section-title` — a `frame-box` around a centered section header.
card` — a padded surface with header/content/footer regions; a card, not a frame.
divider` — one hairline with optional centered label; no corners, no content.
bestPractices: Stack or abut frames with `flush` so a shared edge reads as one hairline instead of two. It subtracts the named sides from this frame's own set, so it works vertically (`flush`, i.e. `top`) and horizontally (`flush="left"`) with the same mechanic.

Use `borders` rather than overriding the border utilities from the call site: `y` for a full-bleed band that keeps only its top and bottom rules, `none` for a cell of a `gap-px` divider grid whose edges are already drawn by the grid's seams.

Keep `marks` on: the corner squares are the frame's identity, and they cost nothing when the rules are handed over to a grid. On a shared edge, pair `flush` with the opposite `marks` keyword (`flush` + `marks="bottom"`, `flush="left"` + `marks="right"`) so the junction carries one rule and one mark per corner.

Reach for `hatch` sparingly — one hatched frame per view reads as texture; several read as noise. For a ruled ground, compose `texture-material` at its `lines` kind inside the frame instead: it is the system's texture layer, and its ink and pitch are tunable from the call site.

props.name: size
props.doc: How much vertical air the gap holds, as a multiple of `--spacing-xxl`: `small` is 1× (keeps two related bands close), `medium` 2× (the ordinary break), `large` 3× (opens a new part of the page). The token is responsive, so every step scales with the viewport.

props.name: hatch
props.doc: Draw the gap's ruled line texture — fine vertical rules at a fixed pitch.

section-gap.purpose: The empty registration frame that divides two page sections. On a page with no margins between sections, this frame *is* the gap: it holds the vertical air, and its own two rules are what separate the sections it sits between — which is why it is a frame and not a spacer `div`. `size` picks how much air, on a three-step scale built from the theme's own spacing tokens.
useWhen: Between two stacked page sections on a full-bleed, framed layout.
Wherever a page needs breathing room that still reads as part of the frame instead of as empty margin.
To change the weight of one break without touching its neighbours — a `large` gap before a new part of the page, `small` between two bands that belong together.
avoidWhen: To space two elements inside a section → use the layout's own `gap-(--spacing-*)` utility.
To draw a single separating line with no air → use `divider` instead.
When the gap must hold content (a headline, a CTA) → use `section-title`, or a `frame-box` you fill yourself.
related: frame-box` — the frame this component configures; reach for it directly when the gap needs content or different rules.
texture-material` — the layer that paints the ruling, composed here at its `lines` kind.
section-title` — the framed header that usually follows a gap; it owns no vertical air of its own beyond its padding, so the gaps around it are what set the page's rhythm.
divider` — a hairline with no vertical air.
bestPractices: Pick the step by what the break means, not by how the page happens to look: `medium` is the ordinary break between sections, `large` opens a new part of the page, `small` keeps two related bands close.
Do not override the height from the call site. The steps are multiples of `--spacing-xxl`, so they already scale with the viewport; a hand-set height freezes one break out of the page rhythm.
Keep one step per break — stacking two gaps to reach a bigger one draws an extra pair of rules.

Let it carry the shared rule: it renders `flush`, so its top rule is subtracted and the section above supplies it instead of doubling it. It still ticks every corner (`marks="all"`): the shared rule is given away, the registration mark is not.
Reach for `hatch` here rather than on a section header: the gap is the one band with no copy of its own, so the texture gives the break identity without sitting behind a headline.

Leave the ruling unmasked. Each line is one solid ink edge to edge and its transparency is the ink's own, so the field reads as ruled page material rather than as a fill that fades out; a vignette on a band this short reads as a smear.
Do not wrap it in a padded container; the gap is the padding.

props.name: orientation
props.doc: Axis the panes are laid out on; horizontal places them side by side, vertical stacks them.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.doc: Accessible name for the group as a whole.

slots.name: default
slots.notes: On the root, the panes and handles in the order they appear. On a pane, its content. The handle takes no slot.

resizable.purpose: A group of adjacent regions whose shared edges the reader can drag. It is the layout primitive behind a workspace — an editor with a terminal under it and a preview beside it — where every region is content the reader is working in and the split between them is theirs to set. It exists because `Sidebar` was being used for both jobs. `Sidebar` is the app's NAVIGATION rail: it collapses to icons, it hides, it is the thing you leave to go somewhere. A terminal, a preview and a code editor are not places you navigate to — they are the work — and dressing two of them as navigation rails made a screen with three "sidebars" and one document, on an axis `Sidebar` does not even have (it has no horizontal edge, so a terminal under an editor had to hand-roll its own splitter). This component owns the EDGE; `Sidebar` goes back to owning navigation.
useWhen: Two or more content regions share an edge the reader should be able to move (editor + terminal, editor + preview, list + detail).
The split is a working preference the reader sets many times in a session, not a one-time layout decision.
A region has to shrink to nothing and come back without losing its state (an editor's undo history, a scroll position).
The layout needs a horizontal edge — one region above another — which no other component in the package provides.
avoidWhen: The panel is the app's navigation rail → use `sidebar`, which owns the icon rail, the collapse and the nav semantics.
The content is a temporary overlay over the page → use `drawer` (a panel that comes and goes) or `dialog`.
The regions have a fixed relationship the reader should not change → use plain flex/grid layout with the layout tokens.
The panel is one scrolling region with no movable edge → use `scroll-area`.
related: sidebar` — the navigation rail. Collapses to icons, hides, and carries nav semantics; reach for it when the panel is how the reader gets somewhere, not what they work in.
scroll-area` — one region that scrolls. A pane usually contains one.
drawer` — a panel that arrives over the page and leaves; a resizable pane is always there.
bestPractices: Give exactly ONE pane in a group no `basis`. That pane absorbs the remaining space, so the group always fills its container and the reader never sees a gap or a scrollbar they did not cause.
Put the `basis` on the pane whose size the reader cares about (the terminal's height, the preview's width) and let the document be the flexible one.

Keep the pane's own state alive when it is collapsed — collapse renders it at zero length, it does not unmount it. A code editor that loses its undo history when the reader drags an edge shut has lost the reader's work.
Give every handle an `ariaLabel` naming the edge it moves ("Resize the terminal"), never the generic default: a screen with three handles otherwise reads as three identical controls.
A control that reopens a collapsed pane belongs OUTSIDE that pane, in the surrounding chrome. A control that only exists inside the thing it hides cannot bring it back.
